sections.body_en:
The process of a woman's purification for her husband consists of three stages: a) hefsek tahara (literally "cessation in purity", the examination establishing that the bleeding has stopped); b) shiv'a neki'im (the seven clean days); c) tevila (immersion).

When the woman estimates that her bleeding has stopped, she should examine herself with a thorough bedika (internal examination) called the 'hefsek tahara'. If the bedika comes out clean of blood, it has been established that her bleeding has stopped, and when the sun sets she may begin counting the first day of the seven clean days. Without the 'hefsek tahara' bedika, even if in practice her bleeding has stopped, she has not left her presumptive status (ḥazaka) of one who is seeing blood, and she cannot begin to count shiv'a neki'im.1

The preferred time for the 'hefsek tahara' bedika is close to sunset, and as long as she examines herself less than two and a half hours before sunset, she is still considered to be examining at the preferred time. But if the sun has set, the next day has already begun, and only at sunset of the following day will she be able to begin the shiv'a neki'im. Therefore, a woman who is concerned that she may forget to examine herself during the two and a half hours before sunset, or that she will be in a place where she cannot examine herself, would do better to perform the 'hefsek tahara' in the morning or at midday, rather than try to be meticulous and perform the bedika at the preferred time at the risk of perhaps losing the day (only in a rare case, which will be explained in the note, is it obligatory to examine close to sunset).2

notes_en.en:
Regarding a zava (a woman who saw blood outside the time of her period), some say that the hefsek tahara bedika is a Torah requirement, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:28): "But if she becomes clean of her discharge" – that is, she has performed the 'hefsek tahara' bedika – "then she shall count for herself seven days, and after that she shall be pure" (Pardes Rimonim; Ḥavot Da'at 196:3; R. Akiva Eiger; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 196:1). According to the Rashbam, Or Zaru'a (part 1, 338) and She'elat David (YD 3), it is rabbinic. Regarding a nidda (a menstruant woman) who immerses at the end of seven days from the onset of her veset (menstrual period), some say that by Torah law she must examine herself before her tevila (Baḥ, Responsa Ha-yeshanot 126; Badei Ha-shulḥan 196:1, s.v. 'bodeket'). And some hold that just as for a zava the bedika is rabbinic, so too for a nidda (Or Zaru'a and She'elat David, ibid.). Regarding a nidda in our times, who conducts herself as a zava: according to those who hold that a zava and a nidda must examine by rabbinic law, so too is the law for a nidda in our times. In addition, even according to the Baḥ (ibid.), who holds that for a zava the hefsek tahara is from the Torah, for a nidda of our times who conducts herself as a zava the hefsek tahara is rabbinic. And some are concerned and hold that since we are stringent to regard a nidda as a possible zava, perhaps the hefsek tahara bedika should be regarded as a possible Torah obligation (see below, note 4; Avnei Shoham 196:1; Mishmeret Ha-tahara 10:3).
The tevila of a nidda is not written explicitly in the Torah, but only the waiting of seven days. In practice it is agreed that the tevila of a nidda (and of a zava) is from the Torah, but the Rishonim disagreed about its source: according to Rav Yehuda Gaon it is learned by a kal va-ḥomer (a fortiori inference) – if one who touches a nidda or her vessels becomes impure and requires immersion (Vayikra 15:19-22), certainly the nidda herself requires immersion in order to become pure. According to Rabbeinu Tam it is learned from the verse (Bamidbar 31:23): "Everything that may go through fire, you shall pass through fire and it shall be clean; nevertheless it shall be purified with the water of nidda," and the Sages expounded (Avoda Zara 75b): "Water in which a nidda immerses" – thus a nidda must immerse in water for her purification. According to the Ri it is learned from the verse (Vayikra 15:33): "And of her who is unwell in her impurity [nidda]," on which they expounded (Shabbat 64b): "She remains in her state of nidda until she enters the water" (the three views are cited in Tosafot, Yevamot 47b, s.v. 'be-makom'). According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 4:3), the Sages derived a binyan av (a general rule from a single case) from the verse (Vayikra 15:18): "And a woman with whom a man lies with emission of seed, they shall both bathe in water and be impure until the evening," that all who are impure require immersion in order to become pure. And according to Rabbi Ḥayim Palti'el (on Vayikra 15:33), a nidda is compared to a zav: just as a zav requires immersion, so does a nidda require immersion.

Close to sunset is the time of 'minḥa ketana' – two and a half proportional hours before sunset (R. Yehuda in the Mishna, Nidda 68a; Gra 196:4; Peninei Halakha: Prayer 24:7, note 9). A bedika after sunset is not effective (Beit Yosef, Baḥ, Perisha, and others). However, in a pressing situation, some say, on the basis of combining doubts, that one may be lenient up to thirteen and a half minutes after sunset (Taharat Ha-bayit p. 277 ff.; see Avnei Shoham 196:1:5). The accepted ruling is not to be lenient in this, for we find that in order for the laws to be clear to all, they were stringent to sit shiv'a neki'im for every drop of blood (above 1:7), and likewise regarding sunset the halakha is clear and definite. However, in a case of especially great need, one may be lenient according to the rules of doubt. And when the doubt is whether sunset had arrived, one may be lenient even when it is not a pressing situation. In these complex questions it is proper to ask a Torah scholar.
Usually it is possible to perform a 'hefsek tahara' only several days after the onset of the veset, and as long as it is performed after the first day from the onset of seeing, according to most Rishonim it may be performed le-khatḥila (from the outset) from the beginning of the day (Ra'avad, Ramban, Rashba, Ran, and others). And some say that if at the beginning of that day she still saw blood, even if it is not the first day of her seeing, the hefsek tahara bedika must be close to sunset (Sidrei Tahara 9; Ḥavot Da'at 1, based on Rashi and Tosafot). In practice it was ruled that le-khatḥila she should examine close to sunset, and when necessary from the beginning of the day (Beit Yosef and Rema 196:1; R. Shlomo Kluger; Maharal Tzintz YD 9; Tiferet Tzvi part 2, 13:3; Leḥem Ve-simla 3, and others). Just as a hefsek tahara in the morning is effective, so too one on the preceding evening is effective for the following day (Ḥadrei De'ah 196:1; Or Le-Tziyon part 1, YD 7).
In the rare case where on the first day of her seeing she has also stopped seeing, and there is also no obstacle to beginning the count on account of the law of 'polet shikhvat zera' (a woman who discharges semen; below, section 5), according to many, since the first day carries the presumption of being entirely impure, only if she performs the 'hefsek tahara' bedika close to sunset and also examines during bein ha-shmashot (twilight) with a mokh daḥuk (a cloth inserted and left in place) can she begin the shiv'a neki'im (Ramban 2:1; Ḥinukh 207; Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 6:20, as interpreted by the Maggid Mishneh and the Beit Yosef; SA YD 196:2, and many Aḥaronim). And some say that a morning bedika suffices (Ra'avad, Rashba and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam). And some say that be-di'avad (after the fact), even without a 'mokh daḥuk' bedika she may begin the shiv'a neki'im, provided that the hefsek tahara is close to sunset (Rema, Levush, Leḥem Ve-simla 4; Taharat Ha-bayit p. 302). Some are stringent that even when her bleeding stopped and she began the shiv'a neki'im and then saw blood again, her law is that of one who sees on the first day (Shakh 196:6). However, in practice, seeing in the middle of the shiv'a neki'im is not considered the first day of her impurity, and her law is like that of seeing from the second day onward (Tiferet Tzvi 196:6; Levushei Oz p. 437).

sections.body_en:
The 'hefsek tahara' bedika must be done with a soft white cloth, so that if blood remains in the vagina it will be visible on the cloth (SA YD 196:6). One should not examine with a white paper tissue, lest it crumble or tear and the bedika be spoiled. However, in a pressing situation when there is no other solution, she may examine with one, taking care that it does not tear. The cloths used for bedika are customarily called 'edei bedika' (examination cloths), and they are sold in supermarkets; already in the days of the Talmud it was customary to sell cloths for bedika (Nidda 17a).

Before the 'hefsek tahara' bedika, the inside of the vagina should be cleaned of remnants of blood with the help of a moist cloth such as an 'ed bedika', for sometimes the bleeding from the uterus has already stopped but remnants of blood remain in the vagina, and without cleaning them the bedika will not come out well.

A woman who is concerned that if she examines with a dry cloth she will injure the vagina may moisten the 'ed bedika' slightly, provided that it is not actually wet, lest the moisture dissolve and conceal a drop of blood. She may likewise smear the vagina with oil, provided she does so some time before the bedika, so that the oil has time to be absorbed into the skin of the vagina and does not cover over the blood.

Before the 'hefsek tahara' bedika it is good to clean the area around that place with a wipe or with water, to ensure that no remnants of blood or dirt remain there which might raise doubts about the bedika. It is likewise good to clean the fingers and to look that there are no remnants of lipstick and the like on them.3

notes_en.en:
A moist wipe is not good for a bedika, because the soap in it may dissolve the blood and fade its appearance. Likewise a tampon is not good for a bedika, because it may absorb the appearance of the blood, and also it is not possible to examine the crevices and folds with it. In a pressing situation when there is no other solution, some are lenient with both.
The Rema wrote (196:3): "It is a proper custom that when a woman makes the hefsek tahara, she bathes… However, if she washed only her lower parts, that suffices." His words were said in days when homes had no showers, toilets or toilet paper, and it was not customary to wear underwear, and there was a reasonable concern that bloodstains and dirt had remained on the body, which, were she to find them after the hefsek tahara, would bring her into doubt. But nowadays, the concern that there will be bloodstains on the body of a woman who is accustomed to clean herself in the accepted manner is negligible, and therefore le-khatḥila it suffices to clean the area around the place with a wipe or with water. In any case, even in the past the custom of bathing was not indispensable, and a woman who was traveling could make do with the hefsek tahara (Levush, Torat Ha-shelamim, and others).
Some say that if she examined herself and found that she was not clean, and immediately cleaned herself and examined again and the bedika came out clean, it is not effective. For it is possible that the menstrual bleeding is still continuing and every few minutes a drop of blood comes out, and this 'hefsek tahara' did not verify that the bleeding had stopped (Ḥazon Ish 81:1). Rather, she should wait a few minutes – le-khatḥila 8, and be-di'avad about 3 (Ḥut Shani 196:4:8). However, from the fact that none of the poskim warned about this common halakha, it is implied that in their view she may make the hefsek tahara immediately after cleaning the vagina (Taharat Ha-bayit p. 274, and Badei Ha-shulḥan 196:1, Bi'urim s.v. 'she-tifsok'. This is also implied by the Gemara, Nidda 14a-b, that whatever is not 'otiyom' [immediately] [?], that is, within about half a minute, is already considered 'after a time', and therefore they are exempt from a sacrifice; consequently she may make the hefsek tahara).

sections.body_en:
To perform the bedika, she must wrap her finger in the cloth, insert it as deep into the vagina as possible without strain, and examine gently in the crevices and folds, that is, press the cloth against all sides of the vagina, so that even if there is blood in the folds of the vagina it will be visible on the cloth. After the bedika she should look at the cloth: if there is blood on it, the bedika is invalid. If none of the impure colors of blood (above 2:3) is on it, even if there are discharges of another color on it, the bedika is valid, and she may begin counting the shiv'a neki'im.

If blood or possible blood is found on the cloth, it is advisable to clean the vagina again with a moist cloth and, still before sunset, to try again to make a hefsek tahara, in order to begin the shiv'a neki'im at sunset. It is therefore advisable to perform the hefsek tahara bedika sufficiently before sunset, so that if necessary there will be time left for another cleaning and a repeat bedika.

A woman who cannot insert her finger into the vagina, such as a virgin, should examine with the cloth up to the place of the hymen (below 8:3). Likewise, a woman who has a wound in the vagina that may bleed during the bedika should examine up to the place of the wound, for the main thing is that she examines as far as is possible for her.4

notes_en.en:
We learned in Nidda 12a that there are two kinds of bedika: wiping between the labia only, and an internal bedika inside the vagina, which must be done gently so as to examine the crevices and folds (Nidda 5a). We further learned in Nidda 41b that blood coming out of the uterus renders impure once it has come out of the cervix and reached the vagina, to "the place where the shamash treads" (the area reached during relations), and from this the Rosh learned (Nidda 10:5) that this is the place of the internal bedika in the crevices and folds. So wrote Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Hagahot Maimoniyot and the Tur. And so is the view of the Razah, Rashba, Ra'ah, Semag and Semak, that the bedika must be deep, in the crevices and folds. Some learned from the Rosh that one must be very stringent regarding the depth of the bedika, up to a place that is difficult to reach; however, it seems that his intent is the depth that can be reached easily, for his warning is: "and not that she insert it a little to wipe herself, for that is called wiping and not a bedika." According to the Ra'avad and the Teruma, the bedikot required for a woman's purification for her husband are bedikot deep in the vagina but not in the crevices and folds, for such thorough bedikot were required only for taharot (ritually pure foods), such as teruma and ḥalla. The Rambam's view is that the bedika required for a nidda is wiping between the labia, and so is the view of the Rif as explained by the Noda Bi-Yehuda (Kamma YD 46), and so was the practice in various communities and in Yemen (Taharat Moshe 13:9-10). According to the Ramban (Nidda 5a), the hefsek tahara bedika must be deep in the vagina, while during the shiv'a neki'im "any bedika at all suffices."
The SA (YD 196:6) ruled in accordance with most Rishonim that the bedika must be "deep, into the crevices and folds." However, one must say that even in their view, when it is not possible to examine deep, one may make do with a bedika as far as possible. Just as a virgin can become pure before her wedding even though she does not examine deep, because the hymenal membrane near the opening of the vagina does not allow it (SA 192:1; Baḥ 4; below 8:3). Indeed, some are stringent that even a woman who very probably has a wound in the vagina must make the hefsek tahara bedika in the crevices and folds (Ḥavot Da'at 196:4; R. Akiva Eiger, Kamma 60; Ḥokhmat Betzalel; and see SA 187:7). However, many hold that when there is concern that she has a wound, she should do a light bedika. Some explained that examining deep and in the crevices and folds is a rabbinic stringency for one who is able, and therefore even according to those concerned that the hefsek tahara bedika is from the Torah, one may make do with a light bedika (Sidrei Tahara 196:23). And some explained that the 'hefsek tahara' bedika is a rabbinic obligation, because by Torah law it suffices that she feels that she has stopped seeing; therefore, when necessary, when it is difficult to perform a thorough bedika, one may make do with a bedika as far as possible (Zikhron Yosef YD 10). Therefore many ruled that a woman who cannot examine deep, because of a wound or because of a ring that in the past used to be placed for a woman suffering from uterine prolapse, should pay attention that her veset has stopped and examine as far as is possible for her. Similarly, a woman who has a wound that may open during the hefsek tahara should examine up to a place that does not bring out blood (Ḥatam Sofer YD 142; Binyan Tziyon 71; She'elat David YD 3; Or Same'aḥ YD 4; Avnei Nezer YD 252; Taharat Ha-bayit part 2, pp. 367-375). When there is doubt whether there is a wound there, she can get the help of a female doctor or nurse to check this.

sections.title_en: Mokh Daḥuk after the Hefsek Tahara
sections.body_en: There is a custom of hiddur (enhanced observance) among women that, in addition to the 'hefsek tahara' bedika, they also perform a 'mokh daḥuk' (a firmly inserted cloth) bedika during bein ha-shmashot (twilight). That is, they place an 'ed bedika' in the vagina, to remain inserted there from before sunset until after the emergence of the stars, so that she will know without any doubt that her bleeding has indeed stopped. The time of sunset is published in calendars, and le-khatḥila the mokh should be left in for close to half an hour. However, it is agreed that the 'mokh daḥuk' custom is a custom of hiddur and is not indispensable.5

notes_en.en: When the 'hefsek tahara' is performed on the first day of seeing, according to many one must take care that the hefsek tahara bedika be close to sunset and also perform a 'mokh daḥuk' bedika (as explained in note 2). But when the hefsek tahara is performed from the second day onward, it is agreed that there is no need to perform a 'mokh daḥuk' bedika, and it is only a custom of hiddur (Rashba; SA YD 196:1; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 17). Beyond the hiddur, the 'mokh daḥuk' bedika sometimes has a halakhic benefit: a) If redness was found on the hefsek tahara, and afterwards a mokh daḥuk was inserted and the mokh came out clean, be-di'avad, even though it was not inserted with a bedika of the crevices and folds, since it was firmly in place for a prolonged time it can serve as a substitute for the hefsek tahara bedika that was invalidated, and by virtue of it she will be able to begin the shiv'a neki'im (Shemesh U-magen part 2, YD 9; Ḥut Shani 196, end of sub-paragraph 7. It should be noted that according to the Ḥavot Da'at 191:8, a mokh daḥuk bedika too must be in the crevices and folds). b) If she forgets to perform a bedika on the first day, be-di'avad she may count the mokh daḥuk as the bedika of the first day (see below, section 8 and note 9). And although some hold that the bedika of the shiv'a neki'im must specifically be by day (Sidrei Tahara 196:19; Tzemaḥ Tzedek), according to many a night bedika is effective (Ḥadrei De'ah, Leḥem Ve-simla, Mahari Ha-levi, Taharat Ha-bayit part 2, p. 328).

sections.title_en: The Law of a Woman Who Discharges Semen
sections.body_en:
In preparation for the Revelation at Mount Sinai, Israel were commanded: "Be ready for three days; do not go near a woman" (Shemot 19:15). The Sages explained that during the three days after union, seed that is capable of conceiving is discharged from the vagina, and therefore its loss is accompanied by impurity; and so that the women too would receive the Torah in purity, the men were commanded to separate from their wives for three days (Shabbat 86b). Likewise, the Sages ruled that when a couple has had union, and some time afterward the woman saw blood and became impure, even if her blood has stopped flowing, as long as there is a possibility that she will discharge from the vagina semen that is capable of conceiving, she cannot begin to count shiv'a neki'im. For the seven days must be clean also of the discharge of semen. But after three full days (72 hours) from the union, the seed has already lost its vitality, and its discharge does not undo the counting of the shiv'a neki'im. There are two main approaches regarding the restrictions derived from this halakha, the approach of the Shulḥan Arukh and the approach of the Rema:

According to the approach of the Shulḥan Arukh (196:11, 13), after three full days from the union one may begin to count shiv'a neki'im. However, since in practice the three full days are spread over four days, only after the end of the fourth day may she begin the seven clean days. That is, if the union was on Sunday, whether at its beginning, on the night of Sunday, which is Motza'ei Shabbat (Saturday night), or at its end before sunset, the three full days will end at the end of Wednesday, and the seven clean days will begin on the night of Thursday (Wednesday night). And even if the bleeding lasted only one hour, she should not begin shiv'a neki'im before then, lest she discharge semen. However, if she wishes to begin earlier, she can remove all the seed remaining in her by cleaning the inside of the vagina with a cloth or by bathing in a bath of lukewarm water, and afterwards she may make the hefsek tahara and begin the seven clean days without waiting until the end of four days from the union. This is the halakha according to most Rishonim, and so was the practice in some of the communities of Sephardic and Eastern origin.6

notes_en.en:
The Sages said (Shabbat 86b) that up to six onot (periods of a day or a night) the seed is still able to conceive, and consequently if it is discharged it undoes the shiv'a neki'im. So ruled the Ra'aviya, Teruma, Yere'im, Ramban, Rashba, Rosh, Semag and others. According to the Rambam (Hilkhot She'ar Avot Ha-tum'ot 5:11-13), the Or Zaru'a and the Meiri, based on their version of the Gemara, only up to three onot is the seed at its full vitality and must be taken into account. The discharge of seed renders impure already when the seed comes out from the area of the cervix into the vagina, even though it has not yet come out of the vagina (Nidda 41b).
According to two important approaches among the Rishonim, the law of polet shikhvat zera does not pertain to a woman's purification for her husband: a) According to the Ra'avad, Riaz and Meiri, the law of polet shikhvat zera pertains only to taharot, for only with regard to taharot is the seed considered impure, whereas for her husband it is not impure and does not interfere with the shiv'a neki'im. And so is the view of the Geonim and the Rif, who did not mention this law. The Ramban and Rashba inclined toward this. Many hold that this is also the view of the Rambam (Taharat Moshe 13:15). b) According to Rabbeinu Tam, the Re'em and the Ra'aviya, polet shikhvat zera undoes the count only when she lay with a zav, for then there is concern that together with the seed a drop of his discharge comes out.
However, according to many Rishonim, a woman who discharges semen during the three full days undoes that day of the shiv'a neki'im on which she discharged it. Therefore only at the end of four days from the union may she begin the shiv'a neki'im. And if she wishes to make the hefsek tahara before then, she can remove all the seed from the vagina by wiping with a mokh or by bathing in a bath of lukewarm water that will also enter the vagina, and afterwards make the hefsek tahara and begin the shiv'a neki'im (Tosafot, Maharam of Rothenburg, Rosh, Eshkol, Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, Semag, Teruma, Rokeaḥ, Mordekhai, Hagahot Maimoniyot, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, and others). So it was ruled in the SA (196:11, 13), and so is the custom of some of the communities of Sephardic and Eastern origin. The Semak was concerned that perhaps there are women who do not know how to wipe and remove all the seed; however, this concern is not mentioned by the rest of the Rishonim. And the Ramban and Rashba even added that, according to what is explained in the Gemara (Nidda 41b), even if she merely got up and walked about, the seed comes out, and she may immediately afterwards make the hefsek tahara, without wiping or rinsing the vagina.

sections.title_en: The Approach of the Rema and of Those Who Are Stringent
sections.body_en:
According to the approach of the Rema, one must always wait five days from the onset of seeing, and only afterwards may she begin counting the shiv'a neki'im. For if the union took place during bein ha-shmashot between Sunday and Monday, there is concern that they will mistakenly think it took place on Sunday and that she may make the hefsek tahara at the end of the fourth day and begin the shiv'a neki'im at the start of the night of Thursday (Wednesday night); whereas in truth the union took place at the beginning of the night of Monday (Sunday night), and the three full days continue into the night of Thursday, so that she can make the hefsek tahara only at the end of Thursday and begin the shiv'a neki'im on the night of Friday (Thursday night). They also did not want to rely on cleaning the vagina, lest it not be cleaned well. Nor did they want to calculate the days from the day on which union took place, lest they forget whether there was a union and when it was. And in order not to create distinctions in the law which might cause confusion, they established that even if there was no union during the entire preceding period, one must never begin shiv'a neki'im before five days have passed from the time the bleeding began, and the day on which the bleeding began is the first of the five.

There were communities in which the custom was to be more stringent, and they began counting shiv'a neki'im only after six or seven days from the onset of seeing blood. And although there is no source for this in halakha, apparently, since for many women the menstrual bleeding lasts more than five days, and there were women who did not perform the 'hefsek tahara' bedika properly and began counting shiv'a neki'im before the bleeding had stopped completely, they established a safeguard that they should not begin shiv'a neki'im before six or seven days had passed from the onset of the veset. However, since this is an excessive stringency, most of the great Torah authorities rejected it. Therefore, the custom of those who are stringent follows the approach set out in the Rema, which was accepted in all the Ashkenazic communities and in many communities of Sephardic and Eastern origin.

It should be noted that generally there is no stringency in this custom, since most women in any case cannot make the hefsek tahara before five days have passed from the onset of their seeing. However, for women who have a short veset there is a stringency in it, and above all it is a stringency for a woman who became impure because of a ketem (bloodstain) or a brief bleeding not within the framework of a veset.7

notes_en.en:
The view of the rabbis of Ashkenaz at the end of the period of the Rishonim was that one must never begin shiv'a neki'im before five days have passed from the onset of bleeding, because of the concern explained above. And in order not to create distinctions between the various situations, they were stringent that even if in practice they had not had relations, they should wait five days from the onset of seeing before counting shiv'a neki'im; consequently it is clear that cleaning the area of remnants of seed is not taken into account. So wrote the Maharil 140, Terumat Ha-deshen 245, the Agur, and the Maharik (Ha-ḥadashim 49), in the name of Rabbeinu Shimshon of Sens. The Rema wrote (196:11, 13) that this is the custom of Ashkenaz, and "whoever breaches a fence, a snake will bite him." This custom also spread to many communities in Eastern lands and of Sephardic origin, as cited in Shulḥan Gavoha 196:27 (Salonika); Zera Emet 1:71 (Italy); Eretz Ḥayim (Sithon) 196 (the Land of Israel).
There were communities in which they were more stringent, and the custom was always to wait six days from the onset of seeing blood, and only afterwards did they begin the shiv'a neki'im. So they practiced in Babylonia and in various communities in Turkey, Tunis and other places. Their reason is that in any case many women do not manage to make the hefsek tahara before then, and in addition, many women are not precise in examining the crevices and folds, and it is doubtful whether they have passed from the presumption of 'seeing' to that of 'not seeing'; by waiting six days, there is a presumption that they have stopped seeing (Ziv'ḥei Tzedek; Rav Pe'alim YD 4:20). And there were communities whose custom was to be even more stringent and to wait seven days before beginning the shiv'a neki'im. So was the practice in the days of the Rishonim in a few Ashkenazic communities (see Maharil, Responsa Ḥadashot 93; Rema 196:13), and so was the practice until recent generations in some of the communities of Morocco (Ateret Avot 34:13) and Djerba (Brit Kehuna YD 50:2), and in most of the communities of Yemen (Taharat Moshe, section 32). It seems that their reason is like the reason for the six-day custom, except that since there are women who see for seven days, they were stringent to always wait seven days. Many explained the custom in additional ways (see Birur Halakha 196:37). According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 11:14), this custom began from an error in understanding the mitzva, and he came out forcefully against it. In practice, most poskim rejected the custom of waiting seven or six days before the shiv'a neki'im, because it involves excessive stringency, as the Rema wrote (196:11) concerning the seven-day custom: "and one who is lenient gains, by bringing himself sooner to the mitzva." And although in many communities of Sephardic and Eastern origin the custom in the past was to wait six or seven days before the shiv'a neki'im, nowadays it is agreed that the custom of those who are stringent is to wait five days, according to the approach of the Rema, and no more, as cited in Netivei Am YD 196; Darkhei Tahara 14:21; Or Le-Tziyon part 1, YD 6.
Even according to the approach of the Rema, at times one is lenient to wait four days: after seeing hymenal blood, the custom is to wait four days, since the separation is due to hymenal blood, whose impurity is rabbinic, and not due to nidda blood (Maharal of Prague; Taz 196:5). And so is the law if she again saw hymenal blood at the second union (Responsa Beit Shlomo YD 1:76; Maharsham 1:210, and others). The Shelah wrote that if they did not have relations before she saw, and if she waits five days she will have to immerse on Friday night following a Yom Tov, she should make do with four days, because the stringency of having the ḥafifa (preparatory cleansing) immediately precede the tevila is more important. So too wrote Torat Ha-shelamim 20. And some were lenient in this even if they had relations before she saw (Sidrei Tahara 42; Ḥokhmat Adam 117:2). From this the Arukh Ha-shulḥan 196:40 and Divrei Malkiel 5:102 learned that whenever there is great need, or a pressing situation, or a matter of mitzva, one may be lenient with four days. And Igrot Moshe (YD part 4, 17:22-24) was lenient in a pressing situation, when the husband must travel for several days, and only if she moves it forward to four days will she manage to immerse before he travels. A further law: if she returned home from tevila and they did not have relations, and she saw blood, many ruled that she may begin the shiv'a neki'im immediately on the next day (Responsa Penei Yehoshua YD 12; Sidrei Tahara 39; Ḥokhmat Adam 117:3; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 39). If they separated because they thought they had become forbidden, they count five days from when they separated (Shevet Ha-levi 6:129:8). And likewise when they separated from relations at the time of the onat veset (the time at which her period is expected).
Is one stringent also in the case of a ketem?: The Teruma and Semak wrote that even a woman who became forbidden because of a ketem must be concerned about the discharge of semen. So too wrote the Rema 196:11. On the other hand, according to the Eshkol, since the prohibition of a ketem is rabbinic, one relies on the lenient views (at the beginning of note 6) which permit counting shiv'a neki'im immediately. In various cases his approach was combined into the halakhic weighing (see Responsa Beit David YD 96; Ḥatam Sofer YD 188; Da'at Kohen 80). According to Rav Ovadia Yosef, one may rely on the view of the Eshkol (Taharat Ha-bayit 13:15, pp. 444-446). And so ruled Rav Rabinovitch. And it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that one may be lenient in this with rinsing or wiping.

sections.body_en:
Many ask whether members of communities that followed the approach of the Rema may change their custom to the approach of the Shulḥan Arukh. It is important to note that this question involves not only a desire to be lenient but also a mitzva-minded aim, for the mitzva of ona (the marital mitzva) is an important Torah mitzva, and every stringency that adds days of prohibition impairs it. Likewise, adding days of prohibition may lead to transgression. In addition, one may say that the Rema's custom was based on a situation in which there were fewer means of cleaning the vagina well, and also some of the women were not learned and there was a reasonable concern that they would err in their calculation; to prevent this they were stringent and set a straight and simple line for all situations. But today it is fitting to return to ruling according to the essential halakha. Moreover, perhaps the custom of the stringent communities is binding in its full stringency in a place where all the members of the community were accustomed to be stringent; but today, when we have been gathered into the Land of Israel, those who are stringent may follow the approach of the Shulḥan Arukh, which is based on the view of most Rishonim.

In practice, despite the strong arguments of those who wish to be lenient, without a broad consensus of rabbis it is not possible to decide on a change of the custom, for education toward the observance of the mitzvot is based to a great extent on preserving traditions and customs.

But when this does not involve a clear change of custom, the couple may take upon themselves the approach of the 'Shulḥan Arukh'. Foremost among these are those of Sephardic and Eastern origin: even if in their community the custom was to be stringent according to the Rema, since in most halakhot the members of their community follow the 'Shulḥan Arukh', it is not a great change if in this halakha too they follow it.

Likewise, when the bride is of Sephardic or Eastern origin and the groom of Ashkenazic origin, they may follow the 'Shulḥan Arukh'. And although it is accepted that the wife follows the customs of her husband, it is possible that in the laws pertaining to women she may continue according to her mother's custom, and especially in this law, where the essential halakha is according to the view of the 'Shulḥan Arukh'.

And if both spouses are of Ashkenazic origin and they very much want to change their custom, they should consult their rabbi about it.8

notes_en.en:
The basis of the argument for changing to the lenient custom is that, according to the rules of halakha, there is no reason to be stringent beyond the approach of the SA. For we learned (in note 6) that according to Rabbeinu Tam, the Ra'aviya and the Yere'im, the law of polet shikhvat zera applies only to a woman who had relations with a zav. And according to the Geonim, Rif, Ra'avad, Riaz and Meiri – and so it is implied by the Rambam, and toward this the Ramban and Rashba inclined – the law of polet shikhvat zera does not pertain to a woman's purification for her husband but only to taharot. And even if we follow the approach of the many Rishonim who hold that the law of polet shikhvat zera applies also to a woman's purification for her husband, nearly all of them agree that it suffices to wait four days, or to clean out the seed and not wait at all. Only a few Rishonim required adding a fifth day, being concerned that she might not know how to clean herself well. It emerges, then, that the approach of the SA accords with the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim, many of whom were even more lenient. In addition, it is possible that the Rema's stringency of not relying on wiping the vagina was in a situation in which cloths and wipes were not plentiful and there was no running water in every home; but today, when it is easy to wash and clean oneself, one can rely on all women to be able to clean the vagina of remnants of seed. And it is possible that the stringency of always calculating five days was based on a situation in which most women did not know how to read and write; but today, when all women know how to read and write, perhaps they would agree with the view of most Rishonim, who were lenient to calculate from the last union and were not concerned that they would err regarding bein ha-shmashot.
To the argument that it is forbidden to change the custom so as not to harm the tradition of Torah, one can respond that the main severity of changing a tradition is where everyone practiced in that way. As the wording of the Sages in Pesaḥim chapter 4: "A place where they were accustomed," and likewise the wording of the Rema here, 196:11: "And so is the custom in all these lands, and it should not be changed"; 196:13: "And whoever breaches a fence in these matters, in a place where they were accustomed to be stringent, a snake will bite him." But when one lives in proximity to righteous Jews who practice otherwise, since it is impossible to say that their custom is not in accordance with halakha, when there are especially strong reasons one may be lenient according to their custom, and there is not much harm to the tradition of Torah in this (and so wrote Si'aḥ Naḥum 86).
Regarding communities of Sephardic and Eastern origin who were accustomed to be stringent according to the Rema: since in general their custom follows the SA, it seems that changing the custom in this area to their general custom of following the SA is not considered a great change. Taharat Ha-bayit 13:12 went further in this; see there. And although many of the great rabbis of Sephardic and Eastern origin ruled to be stringent in this even today (Rav Mordekhai Eliyahu, Rav Ben-Tziyon Abba Shaul; and see Avnei Shoham 196:11:6, pp. 729-734), it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that because of the strong arguments in favor of the approach of the SA, which accords with the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim, and because of the importance of the mitzva of ona (Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato, chapters 1-3), and the concern about stumbling into transgression (ibid., chapter 4), when one of the spouses belongs to the communities of Sephardic or Eastern origin it is proper le-khatḥila that they follow the SA. Also a couple of Ashkenazic origin who returned to observance (ba'alei teshuva), since their parents were not accustomed to be stringent in this, may follow the SA le-khatḥila.
Those of Ashkenazic origin among whom the tradition of the stringency has been preserved continuously, and who very much want to change their custom to the custom of the SA, must consult their rabbi about it. For changing a custom may harm the tradition, but if it is done with consideration of their particular circumstances and with the agreement of their rabbi, this remedies the flaw in changing the tradition. And it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that the more a couple of Ashkenazic origin is connected to a community in which members of all the ethnic groups take part, or has relatives from all the ethnic groups in their close family, the more room there is to take into account their custom of being lenient. In a place of especially great need, such as soldiers who are away from home most of the time, le-khatḥila one should follow the approach of the SA (see above, note 7).
In all the cases in which one moves from the custom of the Rema to the custom of the Shulḥan Arukh, if the couple had already begun to follow the Rema, it is proper that they perform a 'hatarat nedarim' (annulment of vows) for it. It is possible for the husband to go to three people, one of whom is a Torah scholar, to annul it for both of them. He should open by stating that had they known that the stringent custom might be very burdensome for them, they would not have practiced it, and therefore they regret having decided to practice it. On the basis of this opening and the regret, they will permit them to change their custom. However, there is no obligation to annul the vow, for in the annulment of vows of the High Holy Days a declaration is made in advance that all the customs one will practice are not by way of a vow, and since they did not explicitly decide to be stringent in this, the declaration is effective.

sections.title_en: The Seven Clean Days and Their Bedikot
sections.body_en:
The seven clean days are seven full days (twenty-four-hour periods) in which the woman does not see blood, and at their conclusion she may immerse. The twenty-four-hour day begins at the beginning of the night. It emerges that on the same evening of the week on which she began the shiv'a neki'im, she may immerse the following week. For example, if she made the hefsek tahara toward the end of Shabbat and began counting shiv'a neki'im at the end of Shabbat, at the end of Shabbat of the following week she may immerse.

During these seven days the woman must pay attention that she is clean of bleeding, and this attentiveness must be carried out by means of bedikot. Le-khatḥila she should examine herself twice each day, once in the morning and once before sunset. And if this is difficult for her, she should examine herself once each day. These bedikot are done like the 'hefsek tahara' bedika, with a white, soft and absorbent cloth, deep in the vagina, 'in the crevices and folds', that is, pressing the cloth against all sides of the vagina (as explained in section 3, note 4). After the bedika she should look at the 'ed bedika', and if she found the appearance of blood on it, all the days she had counted until then are invalidated, for the seven days must be consecutive. In order to become pure she must again make a hefsek tahara toward evening, and at night begin the counting of seven days anew (SA YD 196:10).

When necessary, a woman for whom even the daily bedikot are difficult may examine herself on the first day and the seventh day only (SA 196:4). Likewise, a woman who sometimes sees ketamim should le-khatḥila examine herself on the first day and the seventh day only (and if there is a wound there, she should examine up to the place of the wound, as explained above, section 3). In a pressing situation, if she examined herself only once during the seven days, in addition to the 'hefsek tahara' bedika, she may be lenient and immerse.9

notes_en.en:
The law of shiv'a neki'im by Torah law applies only to a zava and not to a nidda, and they are meant to separate between the time at which the woman saw blood and became impure and the time at which she may immerse and become pure, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:28): "But if she becomes clean of her discharge, then she shall count for herself seven days, and after that she shall be pure." The Tanna'im disagreed (Nidda 68b) as to how many bedikot are indispensable for the shiv'a neki'im of a zav and a zava: according to R. Eliezer it suffices that they examine on the first and the seventh. According to R. Yehoshua, if they examined on the first and the seventh, these count for them as only two days, for only a day on which one examines is counted. According to R. Akiva, only the seventh day counts for them, for the counting must be consecutive. R. Yossi and R. Shimon ruled like R. Eliezer, that it suffices that they examine on the first and the seventh. The Amora'im disagreed (ibid. 69a) about the approach of R. Eliezer: according to Rav, even one bedika on the first or on the seventh is effective, and according to Rabbi Ḥanina one must examine on the first and on the seventh. Many ruled leniently like Rav (the Geonim, Rambam, Ra'avad, Ramban, Rabbeinu Yona, Rashba, Rosh, Meiri, Ran, Or Zaru'a, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam and others). And some were lenient like Rav regarding the counting of clean days of a nidda nowadays, because it is a stringency that we are strict to regard her as a zava (Razah). Within the approach of Rav, some say that a bedika on one of the middle days is not effective, for only a bedika at their beginning or end indicates a count of seven days (Razah, Ra'ah), and many say that even a bedika on one of the middle days is effective to show that they are clean (Ra'avad, Ramban, Meiri, Rosh, Ran and others). And some ruled like Rabbi Ḥanina (Rokeaḥ), and some took his words into account out of doubt (Semag, Teruma, Mordekhai, Rabbeinu Simḥa).
In note 1 we learned that there is a dispute whether the hefsek tahara bedika is from the Torah or from the words of the Sages. Regarding one bedika of a zava during the shiv'a neki'im, some say that it is from the Torah (Teruma, Tosafot Ha-Rosh and the Ḥinukh. One can explain them as follows: for a zava, whose seeing continues for many days not in the manner of a veset, the Torah required a bedika to prove that she has stopped seeing). And several Aḥaronim wrote that since nowadays niddot are concerned to count like zavot, the Torah obligation of one bedika has also been applied to them (Ḥavot Da'at 196:3; Sidrei Tahara 18; R. Akiva Eiger. And so they inferred from the Beit Yosef, who was stringent like R. Ḥanina because "it is a doubtful karet"). On the other hand, many hold that even the bedikot of a zava are from the words of the Sages, for by Torah law it suffices that she pays attention that she does not feel the emission of blood (Binyan Olam 42; Ḥesed Le-Avraham [Te'omim] YD 58; She'ilat David 2; Leḥem Ve-simla 15. And see note 4, that the view of Zikhron Yosef is that for the hefsek tahara too, by Torah law it suffices that she pays attention that she no longer sees).
Some say that le-khatḥila she may examine on the first and the seventh (Razah, and so it is implied by the Rambam), and according to many Rishonim, le-khatḥila she should examine once each day (Ra'avad, Ramban, Rashba and Rosh), and some say that le-khatḥila she should examine twice a day, in the morning and toward evening (Semag, Semak, Teruma and Rokeaḥ). And so it was ruled in practice in the SA 196:4.
Be-di'avad, the SA (ibid.) inclined to be stringent like Rabbi Ḥanina, that she must examine on the first and the seventh, and if she examined on the first and not on the seventh, she has lost the seven days and must begin to count them anew. Some say that according to this approach she must examine specifically on the first and the seventh (Noda Bi-Yehuda Tinyana 128, and Beit Shlomo 2:41). And some say that she may examine on one of the middle days in place of the first or the seventh (Ḥesed Le-Avraham YD 62; Sefer Yehoshua). And some are lenient even if both days were in the middle of the seven (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 196:25. And according to R. Shaul Natanson in Divrei Shaul, Yosef Da'at, this is preferable). When necessary one may be lenient like their view, since according to most Rishonim one bedika suffices, and according to many of them it may be done on one of the middle days. When necessary, the first bedika may be at the emergence of the stars after the hefsek tahara (above, end of note 5).
A woman who has wounds in the vagina, and there is a reasonable concern that if she examines herself on the first and the seventh she will see blood because of the bedika, should rely on most Rishonim and make do with one bedika (Shev Ya'akov 36; Tzemaḥ Tzedek 123:3; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 196:25-26; Taharat Ha-bayit 13, pp. 328, 335. And see above, section 3, that she should examine up to the place of the wound). Likewise, a woman who sees ketamim because of hormonal pills or an intrauterine device should examine once, according to the view of most Rishonim, so that she does not find them on a cloth in an internal bedika and enter into great doubts (above 2:14).
And likewise, if she forgot and examined only once in the middle of the shiv'a neki'im, in a pressing situation she may rely on the approach of Rav and immerse (Beit David Tebil 2; see Rav Pe'alim YD 2:16). And although many of the Aḥaronim were stringent in these laws, according to the rules of halakha one should be lenient, because according to most Rishonim one bedika suffices, and according to most poskim these bedikot are rabbinic. In addition, one can also treat this doubt as a sfek sfeka (double doubt): perhaps the halakha is like Rav, and even if the halakha is like R. Ḥanina, perhaps she is a nidda and does not need shiv'a neki'im (in a pressing situation one should be lenient and count a mokh daḥuk that remained in place until after the emergence of the stars as one bedika, as explained above, note 5).
If she did not examine on any day, according to many Aḥaronim she cannot immerse at the end of the seventh day, and in principle, since she did not count at all, she has lost all seven days and must begin counting seven days anew. However, in practice, in a pressing situation when it is very difficult for them to be stringent, it is possible for her to examine on the eighth day and immerse, counting the second day after the hefsek tahara as the first day, so that the eighth becomes the seventh; it emerges that she examined on the seventh, and on the night after the eighth, which has become the seventh, she may immerse (Tiferet Le-Moshe). This is because there is no obligation for the shiv'a neki'im to immediately follow the hefsek tahara, and as explained below in note 11, even if she diverted her attention from the counting, these days count for her; thus she can count the shiv'a neki'im from the second day.
[In a pressing situation, when a woman who is not familiar with the halakha comes to immerse and it turns out that she did not do a hefsek tahara bedika and did not do any bedika during the shiv'a neki'im, some instruct her to examine once and immerse. For by Torah law her law is that of a nidda; combined with the reasoning that the feeling that her veset has stopped is effective be-di'avad in place of bedikot, and combined with the reasoning that wiping in the toilet is considered a bedika (see above, note 4). So it is explained in Ashrei Ha-ish YD 1:31:18-19; and also in Ma'ayan Omer 6:75, who added that she should immerse with a berakha; and see Taharat Ha-bayit part 2, p. 499.]

sections.body_en:
After the hefsek tahara bedika she should put on clean underwear that has no bloodstains on it. Likewise, a woman who does not wear underwear at night should check that her sheet and blanket are clean of bloodstains (SA YD 196:3). It is a proper custom to wear white underwear throughout the seven clean days (Rema, ibid.). One can also fulfill this proper custom by means of a white panty liner, and since it is not susceptible to impurity, ketamim found on it will not invalidate the shiv'a neki'im.

A woman who is liable to see ketamim because of wounds in the vagina or the uterus, or because of an intrauterine device or hormonal pills and the like, should from the outset wear colored or black underwear (R. Akiva Eiger, Tinyana 34; Maharsham 1:81).10

notes_en.en:
We find three views among the Rishonim regarding guidance on the garments to be worn during the shiv'a neki'im. a) Many Rishonim wrote that after the hefsek tahara, throughout the shiv'a neki'im, she should wear white garments and spread a white sheet (Semag, Mordekhai, Rokeaḥ, Sha'arei Dura and others). b) Some say that it is proper to wear during the shiv'a neki'im a clean garment without old stains (Teruma, Agur). c) Some did not write any guidance on the matter, even though they wrote out the entire order of the laws of the purity of a nidda; this implies that if she wishes she may wear colored garments (Ra'avad, Ramban and Rashba). And from the view of the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 9:7) it is implied that it is preferable that she wear colored garments.
Some Aḥaronim are stringent and hold like the first view, and in their opinion this is not le-khatḥila guidance but an absolute obligation to wear specifically white during the shiv'a neki'im. Even a woman who has difficulty becoming pure because of ketamim must wear white, since during the shiv'a neki'im she is still under a presumption of impurity, and by wearing colored garments she closes her eyes to the prohibition (Mar'eh Yeḥezkel 50; Levushei Mordekhai Tinyana YD 90). However, it seems that even according to the first view this is le-khatḥila guidance and not an obligation, for the Rosh and the Orḥot Ḥayim wrote in accordance with their view to wear white, but wrote explicitly that it is a custom. And so wrote the Rema (196:3), that it is a proper custom to wear white during the shiv'a neki'im. This implies that when necessary she may wear colored garments. And the SA (ibid.) did not write that she must wear white during the shiv'a neki'im, but rather, like the second view, that she should wear a clean garment – implying even if it is colored. Therefore, a woman who is concerned that she will see ketamim may le-khatḥila wear colored garments, for so is the view of many Rishonim le-khatḥila. And even according to the Rishonim who wrote to wear white, this is a good practice and not an obligation. And so ruled many Aḥaronim, that a woman who has difficulty becoming pure because of ketamim should wear colored garments so that she not become impure (R. Akiva Eiger, Tinyana 34; Maharsham 1:81; Minḥat Shlomo part 2, 70:25; Igrot Moshe YD 2:78; Badei Ha-shulḥan 190:143). And it seems in practice that even a woman who does not have difficulty becoming pure may, if she wishes, wear colored garments, since even according to the Rishonim who guided to wear white, by the essential law there is no obligation in this. And according to many Rishonim there is not even le-khatḥila guidance to wear white (see Taharat Ha-bayit 13:4). Some contemporary poskim, in order to be spared from ketamim, recommended placing in the underwear a liner or pad that is not susceptible to impurity (Orot Ha-tahara 11:30; Mishmeret Ha-tahara 11:4).
Seemingly it is difficult: if the purpose of wearing white during the seven clean days is to see whether there are ketamim that cause prohibition, why, when ketamim are in fact seen, is she guided to wear colored garments or a pad that is not susceptible to impurity? However, it seems that the foundation of the shiv'a neki'im is to pay attention that during these days veset blood or a discharge of ziva (non-menstrual flow) does not continue to come out with sensation; therefore the Sages instituted bedikot, so that through them she will be alert to sensations and to blood, and there is a dispute as to how many bedikot are indispensable (as explained in the previous note). And some of the Rishonim hold that it is proper to heighten the attentiveness by wearing white. But if because of the white garments doubts arise regarding ketamim that come out without sensation, it is preferable to wear colored garments. Also those who hold that le-khatḥila it suffices that she wear examined garments, though not necessarily white, intended by this to heighten attentiveness: for if she finds ketamim on her garment, she will know to pay closer attention lest veset blood is coming out of her with sensation; whereas if she does not wear an examined garment, there is a concern that she will see on her garment an old stain from before the shiv'a neki'im, and her heart will trouble her needlessly lest her blood is continuing to flow (so wrote Torat Ha-shelamim 196:6).
Moreover, even the hiddur in the past was only in wearing a white dress and spreading a white sheet, for the custom of wearing close-fitting underwear arose less than two hundred years ago, when they learned to manufacture fabrics that are both strong and elastic. The significance of this is that when they found a ketem larger than a gris (the size of a bean) on a dress or a sheet, it is reasonable that had they worn close-fitting underwear as in our days, the ketem would have been the size of several gris. For the blood travels a long way from the vagina to the dress or sheet, and many times it would split on the way into several stains on the body and on other places on the garment; therefore, if a stain larger than a gris was found in one place on a white garment, it is reasonable that much more had come out. Therefore it was not common that, because they wore a white dress and spread a white sheet, they became impure because of ketamim, as in our days when they are absorbed on close-fitting underwear. And it is possible that nowadays, even the Rishonim who recommended wearing white would recommend wearing colored garments so as not to enter into the concern of the impurity of ketamim, because their purpose was to pay attention to blood that comes out with sensation within the framework of nidda or zava, and not to catch ketamim.

sections.title_en: Awareness of the Counting of the Seven Clean Days
sections.body_en:
Le-khatḥila the woman should not divert her attention from the counting of the shiv'a neki'im; and even if she saw a color that looked impure and thought that she would have to make a hefsek tahara again, she should not conclude so in her mind, for perhaps it will become clear through the ruling of a Torah scholar that the color is pure, and she will continue the first count. Likewise, if her husband went away on a long trip, she should not stop counting shiv'a neki'im, lest he change his plans and return early. However, be-di'avad, even if in the middle of the seven clean days she thought not to continue counting them, and then again wished to continue counting them, as long as she did not see blood in the meantime she may return to her first count and immerse.11

There is no mitzva to count the seven days verbally, in the way one counts the Omer; all that is required is that the woman remembers that she is in the seven clean days.12

notes_en.en:
Some say that if in the middle of the shiv'a neki'im she thought to stop counting, she can no longer return to her first count, since she diverted her attention from it (Me'il Tzedaka 63; Sidrei Tahara 18; Ḥokhmat Adam 117:12; Ben Ish Ḥai, Year 2, Tzav 17). However, according to most poskim the main thing is that she not see blood, and there is no obligation that her mind be set on counting the shiv'a neki'im; therefore, even if she thought to stop in the middle, as long as she did not see blood she may return to her count. As we find that a woman who has lost her sanity – her friends may examine her and immerse her, and thereby she becomes pure (Nidda 13b; SA YD 196:8). So wrote Shem Aryeh YD 33; Beit David 2; Tzemaḥ Tzedek YD 155:9; Maharsham 3:114, and many others.
If it seemed to her that seven days had passed, but a certain doubt arose for her that perhaps only six had passed, she may be lenient, since her mind inclines toward this, and it is a rabbinic doubt (see Taharat Ha-bayit part 2, pp. 342-345). But in an evenly balanced doubt she should not be lenient, since it was established to apply the law of a zava to a nidda, so that this must be regarded as a Torah-level doubt and one should be stringent (Ḥokhmat Adam 117:15). Moreover, the main purpose of counting seven days is to know their number, and she does not know it.

It is agreed that a zava does not count these seven days with a berakha, because they are not certain, for if she sees blood her count is cancelled (Tosafot, Ketubot 72a, s.v. 've-safra'). But without a berakha, some say that it is a mitzva to count them each day, in the way one counts the Omer, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:28): "then she shall count for herself seven days, and after that she shall be pure" (Ba'alei Ha-tosafot on the Torah; Agudah). The Shelah wrote that even a nidda nowadays, since she is concerned that she may be a zava, must count each day of the shiv'a neki'im, and say at the end of each twenty-four-hour day, before sunset: "Today is the first day of the counting of my libun (whitening)," "Today is the second day of the counting of my libun," and some women are meticulous about this (Ḥokhmat Adam 117:14). And according to most poskim even a zava need not count, for the main thing is that she watches that the days are clean (Ra'aviya, Eshkol, Ha-ḥinukh, Ramban, Ran, Radbaz, Noda Bi-Yehuda Tinyana 123-124, and many others). And this is the custom of the women of Israel, not to count verbally.
